entries.title: Man critically wounded in shooting at Humboldt Park business
entries.summary: <p>A man was left in critical condition after a Humboldt Park shooting Friday evening. </p><p>A 31-year-old man was inside a business in the 4400 block of West Cortez Street at about 7:20 p.m. when he was approached and then shot by an "unknown offender," police said. </p><p>The man was hit in the chest and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, reportedly in critical condition. </p><p>A person of interest in the case was taken into questioning, and a handgun was found at the scene, police said. </p><p>Area detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson, Trump, Obama remember football 'titan' Mike Ditka
entries.summary: <p>Hours before the Willis Towers’ antennas were set to light up in Bears blue and orange to honor Mike Ditka, whose death was announced Friday morning, Mayor Brandon Johnson acknowledged Ditka’s family, the city and “all who love Iron Mike.”</p><p>“Today, we lost a titan of the game and a hero of Chicago,” Johnson wrote in a statement on social media. “Mike Ditka revolutionized football and delivered glory to our great city on and off the field.”</p><p>He was among the dozens of political officials taking to social media to celebrate Ditka’s life.</p><p>Former President Barack Obama posted his own message on X with a photo of himself and Ditka holding up a Bears jersey emblazoned with Obama and the number 85 during a 2011 ceremony honoring the 1985 Super Bowl team at the White House. </p><p>The team’s original trip to the White House to meet Ronald Reagan had been scrapped following the explosion of the Challenger space shuttle that year.</p><p>Obama said that when he arrived in Chicago in 1985, Ditka and the championship team “were king.” It was high praise from a man Ditka once called the “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/3/4/18409790/could-ditka-s-rant-against-obama-end-his-espn-deal" target="_blank" ><u>worst president we’ve ever had</u></a>” while voicing his support for President Donald Trump and former president Ronald Reagan.</p><p>“Coach Ditka set the tone for a team that was punishing, dominant, and fun — and the city loved him for it,” Obama wrote on social media. “I'm thinking of the Ditka family and Bears fans everywhere on the passing of a legend.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">When I got to Chicago in the summer of 1985, Mike Ditka and the Chicago Bears were king. Coach Ditka set the tone for a team that was punishing, dominant, and fun — and the city loved him for it. I'm thinking of the Ditka family and Bears fans everywhere on the passing of a… <a href="https://t.co/RKlJsahYbR">pic.twitter.com/RKlJsahYbR</a></p>— Barack Obama (@BarackObama) <a href="https://x.com/BarackObama/status/2108641562431197517?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Trump, who was informed of Ditka’s passing during a news briefing Friday, said the late coach was “great” while touting his support while he was alive.</p><p>"He was a great guy,” Trump told reporters. “He was with me all the way. He was tough. That's a sad one.”</p><p>Illinois officials posted their own tributes to “da coach,” as U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin called him in his message. Durbin, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/senator-dick-durbin-reelection" target="_blank" >announced last </a>year that he would step down after five terms in the U.S. Senate and seven terms in the U.S. House, said Ditka coached with “style, grace, and respect for the game.”</p><p>“No Bears fan will ever forget the day when the Monsters of the Midway triumphed over the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XX,” Durbin said in a social media post. “Loretta and I will be praying for his family, friends, and former players as well as the millions of Chicagoans and Bears fans in mourning.”</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker wrote on social media that "Da Coach was not only an icon in Chicago, but the entire football world. Our thoughts are with Mike Ditka’s family, friends, and Bears fans today. May his memory be a blessing."</p><p>“Few people are as synonymous with Chicago as Mike Ditka,” Sen. Tammy Duckworth said in her own statement on social media. “Illinois will miss him dearly, but his legacy will never be forgotten. My heart goes out to his family and everyone who loved Da Coach.”</p><p>Longtime political consultant and former Obama advisor David Axelrod also expressed condolences for Ditka while sharing a story of filming a political campaign ad with him for former Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley.</p><p>“When he popped in to do the spot, I started to explain what we were going for,” Axelrod wrote. “He looked at me with a withering stare and said, ‘Just turn on the F-ing camera. entries.title: Blackhawks' Frank Nazar suspended two games for hit on Islanders' Bo Horvat
entries.summary: <p>Blackhawks forward Frank Nazar received a two-game suspension Friday, marking the first time a Hawks player has been suspended since 2021. </p><p>Nazar got the news Friday after a phone hearing with the NHL's department of player safety regarding his check to Bo Horvat's head in the final minutes of the Hawks-Islanders game Thursday.</p><p>Horvat was in the process of nailing the Hawks' empty net from long range — and did have his head down and out — when Nazar gave it a direct blow while skating by. </p><p>The hit incited a brawl, and Islanders coach Pete DeBoer later said Horvat was being evaluated for injury. Nazar received a match penalty, which was inconsequential with the game out of reach and about to end.</p><p>The suspension, which will sideline him Saturday against the Hurricanes and Tuesday against the Penguins, poses a much bigger problem for the Hawks.</p><p>He'll join injured veterans Teuvo Teravainen and Andrew Mangiapane on their list of unavailable forwards, likely prompting another AHL call-up.</p><p>Nazar, who has three points in five games this season, will also forfeit over $68,000 in salary due to the suspension.</p><p>He's the first Hawk to get suspended since former forward Brett Connolly received a four-game ban for interference on former Stars forward Tanner Kero — who was stretchered off after the incident — in December 2021.</p>

entries.title: Mike Ditka inspired comedic gold. But the funniest riff was Ditka as Ditka.
entries.summary: <p>Mike Ditka could bowl over a linebacker, make a sensational catch, motivate his players to greatness, dress down a reporter, out-heckle a heckler, sell you a refrigerator, coach “The Refrigerator,” and make an entire city laugh without ever telling a joke.</p><p>And then he’d have a cigar.</p><p>While Mike Ditka’s primary and iconic legacy as a football player and coach is celebrated elsewhere on these pages, let’s also give Ditka his due as a personality and a performer who starred in dozens of local and national commercials, appeared on “Saturday Night Live” and “Cheers,” and proved to be a worthy comedic partner to Will Ferrell on the big screen.</p><p>This list of football greats turned actors is extensive and impressive, from Jim Brown and Alex Karras to Don Meredith to Merlin Olsen, from Dick Butkus to Fred Dryer, from Terry Bradshaw to Peyton Manning to Nnamdi Asomugha. But whereas we could buy into Jim Brown playing Robert Jefferson in “The Dirty Dozen,” or Fred Dryer as “Hunter” and Merlin Olsen as “Father Murphy,” or even Peyton Manning as Coach Gary on “Modern Family,” Ditka almost always played <i>Ditka</i>.</p><p>On rare occasions, Ditka portrayed a fictional character — for example, “Coach Mafferty” on a couple of episodes of “3rd Rock from the Sun” in 1997, and the mayor of Chicago in a Make-A-Wish Foundation short film project called “Madzilla!” in 2014 — but from episodes of “L.A. Law,” “Coach,” “Becker” and “Entourage,” among other series, the coach played a lightly fictionalized version of himself, and invariably stole the scene.</p><p>It made sense. Ditka was just going to swallow any character whole anyway. How could you script somebody more alpha, more intense, more intimidating, more complicated, more hilarious and more memorable than the real Mike Ditka?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> (One of my favorites: the 1988 “Calling Me Home, Chicago” tourism ad, with Butkus returning home and surprising Ditka at Butch McGuire’s, and the two exchange the simplest and most profound greetings: “Butkus.” “Ditka.” Pure gold.)</p><p>Unscripted Ditka was also magnificently unpredictable, whether he was heckling back at hecklers at press conferences or on sports talk radio, donning roller skates and barreling through the Bears’ offices after dubbing Minnesota’s old indoor arena “The Rollerdome,” or racing through “Take Me Out to the Ballgame” at Wrigley Field in a land-speed record of 22 seconds in 1998.</p><p>The most complete meta-Ditka performance came in the 2005 comedy “Kicking and Screaming,” in which Will Ferrell’s quintessential suburban dad, Phil Weston, recruits Ditka to be the assistant coach for Phil’s son’s youth soccer team. It’s a fully realized role, with Ditka leaning into his hot-tempered persona to mine tremendous laughs. (In our two thumbs up review of the film on “Ebert & Roeper,” I said Ditka deserved a sitcom deal based on this performance; Roger noted, “Ditka is playing himself, and playing himself as nobody else could, and he gets laughs out of just turning and looking at Will Ferrell.”)</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d10000" name="html-embed-module-d10000"></a><iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/B9NO24hbe8Q?si=UwX-y2oKeB5WI5YT" title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe> </div> </div><p>On a personal note, I had the privilege of narrating a live reading of the unproduced “Superfans” movie script written by Robert Smigel and Bob Odenkirk, the creators of that legendary series of sketches. In an Instagram post on Friday, Smigel told the story of 2001 ESPN roast of Ditka where Ditka eschewed the traditional rebuttal: “The whole event was a benefit for Misericordia, a residence where … children and adults with intellectual disabilities are provided personalized care … Coach Ditka used his time to talk about … what Misericordia provides. He could’ve gotten huge laughs firing back at all of us but he cared much more about Misericordia.”</p><p>The live reading of “Da Bears Movie Dat Wasn’t” was staged at the Park West in June of 2010, with performers including Smigel, Odenkirk, George Wendt, Joe Mantegna, David Koechner, my Sun-Times colleague Rick Telander, Keith Van Horne and Ryan Dempster — but it was Dikta as Ditka who stole the show.</p><p>As he did every time.</p>

entries.title: Reopened probe into CPS Board president candidate’s alleged inappropriate contact with teen could end soon
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Public Schools’ inspector general could soon issue findings in its recently reopened investigation into whether Hilario Dominguez, a candidate for Chicago School Board president, acted inappropriately with a 17-year-old in 2017.</p><p>Investigators interviewed the woman, who is now 26, in late September and reinterviewed Dominguez on Tuesday.</p><p>The woman <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/10/02/cps-watchdog-school-board-president-candidate/" target="_blank" ><u>told the Chicago Tribune</u></a> and other media outlets that Dominguez asked about her dating life while they were alone in a car, and he once lifted her up in a hug and spun her around. At the time, Dominguez was 24 and an organizer at The Resurrection Project, a Pilsen-based nonprofit, while she was a CPS student working there through the city’s summer jobs program.</p><p>The woman <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/10/07/chicago-public-schools-watchdog-reopens-inquiry-into-hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>told Chalkbeat and Block Club Chicago</u></a> that the hug with her body pressed against his made her feel “very uncomfortable” and that the car interaction was “really alarming” because Dominguez “was a figure of authority that I trusted.” She also said the concerning behavior stopped after she complained to an adult staffer.</p><p>The young woman has personal ties to Dominguez’s former political rival, Aida Flores, according to several sources. Dominguez denies the allegations and says they are politically motivated.</p><p>“For me, this is beyond a political campaign,” he told WBEZ. “This is about how I hold my head up high in the neighborhoods and in the city that raised me.”</p><p>The school district’s watchdog first opened an investigation into the alleged incidents in 2021 when Dominguez was teaching in CPS. He left that position in 2022 to work as deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union, which endorsed Dominguez in the school board race.</p><p>Earlier this year, the inspector general’s office determined the allegations were unsubstantiated, according to an email sent by an investigator to Dominguez reviewed by WBEZ. But the office recently reopened the case.</p><p>Inspector General Philip Wagenknecht would not comment on why, but the woman<b> </b>told the Tribune that she reached out to his office because <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/10/06/school-board-candidates-contenders-conduct/" target="_blank" ><u>she was not interviewed for the original investigation</u></a>.</p><p>These accusations have been thrust into Chicago’s heated <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/president/" target="_blank" ><u>school board president contest</u></a>.</p><p>Jessica Biggs, one of Dominguez’s opponents in the race, said the alleged conduct was “deeply concerning” and that women and girls in CPS are paying attention.</p><p>“They deserve to know that the next leader of the CPS Board of Education will take their experiences seriously,” she said.</p><p>One of Biggs’ staffers, Alaina Hampton, said in a statement that she has known the woman for years and was long aware of the allegations. Hampton said the woman reached out to her in early September when the inspector general informed her the case was closed. Hampton recommended the woman hire a lawyer. Hampton said she would “continue to stand in solidarity with victims and survivors.”</p><p>Hampton was part of a high-profile sexual harassment lawsuit filed in 2018 against the Democratic Party of Illinois and others. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/11/29/20988763/alaina-hampton-federal-lawsuit-madigan-quinn-settlement" target="_blank" ><u>She settled that case</u></a>.</p><p>Through her lawyer, the woman declined to respond to questions from WBEZ. But she has said she is speaking out now because she wanted to tell her own story. <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/video/local/inappropriate-behavior-alleged-against-school-board-president-candidate/3998741/" target="_blank" ><u>She told NBC Chicago</u></a> that Dominguez’s entries.title: 5th beluga whale dies at Shedd Aquarium
entries.summary: <p>Another beluga whale rescued from the Marineland of Canada has died, the Shedd Aquarium announced Friday.</p><p>Caspian is the fourth rescued beluga to die at the Chicago aquarium since their initial arrival in July, joining eight resident whales. A resident beluga at the Shedd, Beethoven, also died recently at 34, likely due to age-related issues, the aquarium said.</p><p>Five belugas rescued from the Canadian aquatic park have died in total, out of 30 rescued. One taken in by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/09/18/3rd-beluga-dies-marineland-canada-shedd-aquarium" target="_blank" ><u>Oceanografic Valencia in Spain</u></a>, died last month.</p><p>The succession of deaths in less than three months has made it clear that the rescued whales were “made vulnerable by chronic and severe illness,” Shedd spokesperson Johnny Ford told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>Limited diagnostic information available about the rescued belugas made it difficult to determine which were most at risk, Ford said.</p><p>Caspian’s condition “crashed” earlier this week, the aquarium said, and she was kept on life support for nearly four hours in an attempt to save her.</p><p>The deterioration of Caspian and the aquarium's “intensive efforts” to save her deepen the mystery of what ailed the animal. Blood samples examined this week showed abnormalities in both her electrolyte levels and blood pH, according to a statement from the Shedd.</p><p>Her blood pH showed it had become "dangerously acidic," revealing a clearer picture of how sick she was, the statement said. But the information doesn’t help determine what led to her death.</p><p>“Caspian’s loss is felt deeply by the people who knew and cared for her and by those who followed her story,” the statement said. “Our team worked to give her every opportunity to recover. We will share what her examination adds to our understanding with the same care and openness.”</p><p>Peekachu, a 23-year-old female, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/26/one-of-the-shedds-rescued-beluga-whales-has-died" target="_blank" ><u>died Aug. 25</u></a>, and Rain, a 20-year-old female, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/09/03/shedd-aquarium-beluga" target="_blank" ><u>died Sept. 2</u></a>. Osiris, a 26-year-old female, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/09/21/3rd-beluga-whale-dies-shedd-aquarium-moved-marineland-canada-niagara-falls" target="_blank" ><u>died Sept. 2</u></a>1. The rescued beluga in Spain, Jelly Bean, died Sept. 18.</p><p>Reports conducted so far on the other whales showed they had preexisting, chronic conditions.</p><p>Final reports on the deaths of Peekachu and Rain showed major chronic inflammation in their digestive systems, among other issues like hypertension, liver tissue death and lung scarring.</p><p>Experts said these conditions could have elevated their risk of cardiovascular stress, according to the Shedd’s statement.</p><p>Preliminary investigations into the death of Osiris identified chronic liver disease, but her report is unfinished.</p><p>Animal rights activists in the United States and Canada have questioned whether the belugas were healthy enough to endure the stress of being transferred out of Marineland — in trucks and then airplanes.</p><p>"Five dead belugas tells us that after years of neglect at Marineland, these whales were not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport,” said Camille Labchuk, executive director of Animal Justice, a Toronto, Canada-based animal rights advocacy group. "It's heartbreaking that Marineland was allowed to rush through this transfer operation to clear the way for its lucrative land deal. Marineland had years to plan for their retirement to a sanctuary, but failed to do so. Now, the whales are paying the price."</p><p>The rescued belugas were allegedly living in poor conditions at the shuttered aquatic park in Canada, just south of Niagara Falls.</p><p>Shedd is part of a consortium of four U.S. aquariums, as well as Oceanografic in Spain, that together agreed to take the belugas languishing in Marineland. The park closed to the public in 2024, citing financial troubles.</p>

entries.title: Downers Grove North beats Lyons to clinch a share of the West Suburban Silver title
entries.summary: <p>As the postgame celebrations wrapped up on the Downers Grove North sideline on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/10/08/high-school-football-scores-week-8" >Friday</a> after the No. 19 Trojans knocked off No. 22 Lyons 17-10, a fan yelled: “Great job, Horeni!”</p><p>The compliment was for Downers Grove North coach Joe Horeni. These days, it is rare to hear a fan say anything positive about a coach, much less at the top of their lungs.</p><p>“I did a double-take,” Horeni joked. “I don’t know who it was, but I appreciate it. I know my family is already gone.”</p><p>Horeni has built one of the state’s best defenses. He has multiple coaches on staff with decades of experience and a group of players who pay attention to the details that make the difference on key plays, like Downers Grove North’s goal-line stand at the end of the first half.</p><p>“[Lyons] mixes up their looks a lot but they keep the same personnel, so it is hard to tell what they are going to do,” Trojans safety/running back Grant Georgas said. “We were prepped really well all week, studying film and stuff like that.”</p><p>Downers Grove North (7-1, 5-1 West Suburban Silver) forced a fumble on the goal-line stand at the end of the second quarter, and defensive end Declan Davies fell on the ball to end the threat.</p><p>Davies and the Trojan defense held Lyons star running back EJ Kuhlman to 84 yards on 26 carries. Kuhlman’s five-yard run late in the third quarter was the Lions’ only touchdown.</p><p>Downers Grove North has allowed just 61 points all season.</p><p>“It really takes a lot of camaraderie and togetherness, especially on the defensive side of the ball,” Davies said. “Especially in the red zone. entries.title: Kankakee QB Phillip Turner dazzles in win against rival Crete-Monee
entries.summary: <p>Ever since last year's game against Crete-Monee didn't go his way, Kankakee quarterback Phillip Turner has been antsy for the rematch.</p><p>For the senior, it was well worth the wait.</p><p>Turner broke off two dazzling touchdown dashes early, getting the No. 20 Kays off and running en route to a 34-14 win Friday night in Crete.</p><p>Davion White had a 70-yard strip-and-score 66 seconds after Turner's second TD as Kankakee (6-2, 5-0 Southland) opened a 21-0 lead less than two minutes into the second quarter.</p><p>Crete-Monee (6-2, 4-1) got within a touchdown, but the Kays sealed it with late rushing scores by 280-pound defensive tackle Jyheir Sutton and Lebron Campbell.</p><p>The highlight-reel TDs, though, belonged to Turner. On the first, he zigged and zagged his way through the Warriors defense for a 28-yard score. The second was an 83-yard sprint down the left sideline.</p><p>He had 138 rushing yards at halftime and finished with 144 on nine carries.</p><p>"This game's big definitely for us and me personally, too," Turner said. "Last year I got hurt [broken finger] during this game, so I took it personal. ... I think I did what I had to do."</p><p>"I just knew Phil was going to have a big game," Kankakee coach Ed Hazelett said. "Ever since last Saturday he was on a different level. He was tuned in and locked in."</p><p>With the IHSA playoffs on the horizon, Hazelett was mindful not to push Turner more than necessary.</p><p>"He missed a game [earlier in the season] because he had an injury," Hazelett said. "He's still battling a hamstring injury. So we're just kind of working on that day by day, week by week. But he's getting better and stronger as the season goes on."</p><p>Getting White's defensive touchdown right after Turner's second score gave Kankakee the cushion it needed to withstand Crete's comeback.</p><p>Turner's reaction?</p><p>"Oh yeah, I was turnt, I was turnt," he said. "Defense giving us a touchdown ... that's great because that's points that we don't have to score."</p><p>"Our coach, he told us, 'Go for the ball,'" White said. "... So that's what I did. [The Crete ball carrier] was standing up, so I just came for the ball, ripped it out and picked it up and went to the end zone."</p><p>Crete rallied with a diverse and unconventional offense. Dominic Jackson, a 5-11, 250-pound senior who starts on the defensive line, also starts on offense, taking shotgun snaps and lining up at tailback. He rumbled for 119 yards on 18 carries and even threw an eight-yard TD pass to fellow defensive lineman Kamal Bryant on fourth down.</p><p>Amarre Carey added 88 yards on 22 carries for the Warriors, who attempted only two passes all night, Malik Hernandez had Crete's other TD on a 56-yard pick-six that caromed off a Kays receiver.</p><p>The Warriors had other chances. They turned the ball over on downs at the Kankakee three-yard line on its first possession of the night and had another turnover on a high snap when they were driving and down just 21-14 early in the fourth quarter.</p><p>"You can't win games if you turn the ball over," Crete coach John Konecki said. "... I've coached a lot of football games. Those things happen. I'm not going to excuse it away, but these are going to be wonderful learning opportunities."</p>

entries.title: York's Brayden Byford displays rare two-way abilities
entries.summary: <p>If you think of linemen as lumbering types who just rely on brute force to get the job done, consider York senior Brayden Byford.</p><p>The 6-foot, 240-pounder, who is committed to Dayton, starts both ways for the Dukes and his skill set is unusual for his position.</p><p>“He’s not the biggest kid,” York coach Don Gelsomino told the Sun-Times. “. . . He’s got a thick build, he’s very strong. He’s also quick.</p><p>“. . . He was actually a gymnast all through growing up. So once in a while we’d be in the weight room and it’s next to our gymnastics area. He’d go do [back] flips and stuff and it’s kind of crazy. You don’t expect it, but he’s an incredible athlete.”</p><p>In fact, Byford did gymnastics through sixth grade and also played baseball through his sophomore year.</p><p>When he reverts to gym mode every once in a while, it definitely makes an impression.</p><p>“A bunch of people are surprised when they see it,” he told the Sun-Times. “It’s really fun to just go do a backflip and people are amazed.”</p><p>Though it’s his ticket to college, Byford came to football later than most.</p><p>“My parents wouldn’t really let me play before middle school,” he said. “And then our season got canceled because of COVID.”</p><p>But now he’s good enough to be a two-way starting lineman, a rarity in Class 8A where most teams have enough depth to play platoon football.</p><p>Byford is a two-year starter on offense who was rotated in on defense as a junior. Now he rarely comes off the field.</p><p>“He’s a smart kid, he’s in great shape,” Gelsomino said.</p><p>Even so, York coaches do try to keep Byfprd as fresh as possible.</p><p>“If he needs a little rest here or there, [we] make sure we don’t kill him in practice,” Gelsomino said. “. . . It’s a tough workload, but he’s prepared his body for it really well. . . .</p><p>“He’d probably never leave the field but sometimes we actually step in and say, ‘Hey, you’ve got to sit out a few plays here.’ ”</p><p>“It’s a lot playing both ways,” Byford said. “[It’s about] managing, whenever you get a chance to come off the field, make sure to breathe and drink water.”</p><p>Byford and the Dukes remain in the West Suburban Silver race after earning their biggest win of the year last week, 18-17 in overtime against previously unbeaten Downers Grove North.</p><p>Another tough test awaits on Saturday when York (4-3, 2-2) travels to Glenbard West (5-2, 3-1).</p><p>Last week’s win followed a pair of three-point conference losses.</p><p>“I think it really helps because our losses to Hinsdale [Central] and [Oak Park] — really, it got a few people down,” Byford said. “We just had to keep chugging forward and keep our heads up and make sure that we knew what we were doing.”</p><p>He’s focused on the end of the regular season and then the playoffs, but there is more football in his future at Dayton.</p><p>“I did a bunch of camps before junior season and I got a little bit of interest, but nothing too major,” Byford said.</p><p>There were more camps before this<br>season. Dayton was the first one, and it led to an offer.</p><p>“When I got the call, I was jumping for joy,” said Byford, who later added another D-I offer from St. Thomas. “It was fantastic.”</p><p>He understands how he beat the odds in the current recruiting environment.</p><p>“There’s a lot of [college] teams that are just looking at the transfer portal right now and they’re not taking guys out of high school, which is really a shame.”</p>

entries.title: Bulls’ frontcourt injuries throw a little cold water on preseason fun
entries.summary: <p>The NBA preseason is a time for daydreaming about what might be. And this particular Bulls season raises more exciting ‘‘what-ifs’’ than usual.</p><p>What if hotshot rookie Caleb Wilson, whom the Bulls drafted No. 4 overall, turns out to be the real deal? What if forward Matas Buzelis makes a proper third-year leap? What if the Wilson-Buzelis tandem shows itself as a foundation to build on? Wouldn’t that be nice?</p><p>On Friday against the Grizzlies, however, the Bulls got to ponder a more sobering possibility: What if they have to play without their big men?</p><p>The Bulls’ two centers, Zach Collins (quad) and Nic Claxton (hamstring), are dealing with injuries that have kept them out of training camp. Against the Grizzlies, a third big man was added to the list: Jalen Smith sat out with soreness in his left foot.</p><p>In addressing the hole in the frontcourt, coach Tiago Splitter — not a small man himself — kept it real.</p><p>‘‘It is a concern,’’ he said before the Bulls’ 104-100 loss. ‘‘I’ve gotta be honest with you. We’ve gotta be careful with their minutes throughout the season. We probably do have to have every night, like, a three-man rotation at [center].</p><p>‘‘It’s a little bit what the league is also asking, the way the league is playing — physical, fast. Sometimes a 7-footer cannot play for 35 minutes, so you’ve gotta divide those minutes with three big men running up and down.’’</p><p>Sounds like a reasonable plan for when all three return in the regular season. But there’s no guarantee of a full bill of health at the position, especially given that Collins and Claxton have been bogged down by injuries in recent years.</p><p>That might spell trouble in the paint. Tobe Awaka, an undrafted rookie who had to start at center, barely measured up to Grizzlies center Zach Edey’s shoulders. Grizzlies rookie Cameron Boozer — drafted one slot ahead of Wilson at No. 3 — consistently outmuscled the Bulls’ wings. The Bulls offered no real resistance down low — and this was against the rebuilding Grizzlies.</p><p>Yes, frontcourt depth is something for Splitter to worry about in the short term. But the Bulls are in the beginning stages of a rebuild. The real hope and excitement is about the future. And the vision built around young players flashed a little promise Friday.</p><p>Wilson found his three-point stroke after a difficult first half, going 5-for-11 from deep and finishing with 21 points. Buzelis got into his mid-range bag before leaving with an ankle injury. Even rookie Dailyn Swain, who struggled in Summer League and is getting a chance at point guard with Tre Jones out, looked a little more comfortable running the offense.</p><p>It’s just a matter of getting the whole system to click.</p><p>‘‘Knowing the team that we have, our roster, young guys, we want to play fast, but we still want to be organized,’’ Splitter said. ‘‘Still want to have good shots. Touch the paint. Try to create advantage that way and then spray the ball out.</p><p>‘‘Win the possession game, rebound game, take care of the ball and create turnovers.”</p><p>After the Bulls’ preseason opener Tuesday against the Suns, Splitter said the team was ‘‘far from where we want to be with quick decisions and quick reactions.’’</p><p>That continued to be an issue Friday. Turnovers halted fast breaks, and the half-court offense flowed only here and there.</p><p>‘‘I don’t like how we started,’’ Splitter said. “We were stuck in mud. Slow thinking, slow feet. Not aggressive enough. Third quarter was much better. That’s how we’ve gotta play.”</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Guard <b>Jaylin Sellers</b> missed the game with soreness in his back.</p><p>• Bulls legend <b>Scottie Pippen</b> was in the house to watch his son, Grizzlies guard <b>Scotty Pippen Jr.</b></p>

entries.title: My first home, CHA's LeClaire Courts, readies for a new beginning
entries.summary: <p>Fifty-seven years ago this month, my mother brought me home from Michael Reese Hospital, where I was born, to 4907 W. 43rd St. in the LeClaire Courts public housing development on Chicago’s Southwest Side.</p><p>She lived there in a two-bedroom apartment with my grandparents and her two younger sisters, who were 14 and 11 at that time. Her older brother was in the military. My grandparents stayed in one bedroom; my mother, her sisters and I stayed in the other bedroom.</p><p>It was tight quarters, for sure, but LeClaire Courts was actually a come-up for my grandparents. Before they moved there in the mid-1950s, and before my youngest aunt was born, the family lived out of one bedroom in a large first-floor apartment of a graystone two-flat they shared with other family members in Bronzeville. It was a typical story for Black folks who made their way to Chicago during the second wave of the Great Migration. Someone would make the trek and establish roots in Chicago, and other family members would follow.</p><p>When I was born, my mother worked for a printing company in the South Loop. Once she was able to afford her own place, when I was 3 years old, we moved from LeClaire Courts to a third-floor apartment of a three-flat in Auburn Gresham. I lived there until I went away to college, but I’d often visit relatives — my grandparents and later an aunt and my cousins — in LeClaire Courts.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e70000" name="module-e70000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>I don’t remember my earliest years there, as an actual resident, but I have vivid memories of the many summers, spring breaks, Christmas breaks and countless weekends and holidays I spent there. I absolutely loved the place — so much so that when I drove past the development in 2011 and noticed it was being demolished, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/race-class-communities/2022/01/27/reflections-on-living-in-leclaire-courts-public-housing" target="_blank" ><u>I had to stop and take pictures and videos</u></a>. I even crossed over boundaries meant to keep people off the premises and <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ciqNFJVs9gU" target="_blank" ><u>walked through the apartment where my aunt and cousins once lived</u></a>. I was too late to visit the building where my grandparents lived and where I’d lived as a small child. It had already been torn down.</p><p>I hadn’t walked the grounds there since the summer of 1982, just before my aunt and cousins moved away. In the three decades that followed, the development fell on hard times — and census data shows just how hard.</p><p>LeClaire Courts is part of a census tract about a mile north of Midway Airport. That census tract sits just west of Cicero Avenue and south of the Stevenson Expressway from 43rd Street to 47th Street. Within that census tract, the development sits north of 45th Street and a small community of single-family homes — an area we referred to simply as “the homes” when I was kid — sits to the south.</p><p>When my grandparents moved there, LeClaire Courts was a working-class, racially integrated community. In 1970, a year after I was born, the census tract where the development is located was still racially integrated — 64% Black and 35% white. By 1980, however, the census tract was 97% Black.</p><p>In 1970, among those 25 years or older, about 3% of residents in the census tract had at least four years of college or a bachelor’s degree. By 2011, the figure had increased to just 6%. Citywide, that figure grew from 8% to 33% during the same span.</p><p>In 1970, the unemployment rate in the census tract was 7.7%. In 1990, it was 25.8%. In 2000, it was 22.7%. The region’s loss of manufacturing jobs may have contributed to the spike in the census tract’s jobless rate. In 1970, more than 37% of its working residents worked in manufacturing. It was just under 15% in 2000.</p><p>In 1980, the citywide median household income was $15,301. It was $14,643 in the census tract where LeClaire Courts is located. However, by 2020, the citywide median household income had more than doubled to $38,625. Meanwhile, it was just $16,691 in the census tract surrounding the development.</p><h3>Lack of investment, opportunity</h3><p>According to The Chicago Reporter, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development praised LeClaire Courts in the early 1990s <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoreporter.com/dumping-grounds/" target="_blank" ><u>as the lowest-crime development in the </u></a>Chicago Housing Authority. But an analysis of city data shows that homicides at the development increased from 11 in the 1990s to 17 in the 2000s — with five murders alone in 2002 — as the development’s population declined and it started receiving residents moving from other developments slated for closure.</p><p>Like many public housing communities, LeClaire Courts succumbed to poverty, drugs, crime and violence. In the eyes of many, that’s the story of public housing. But that’s not the LeClaire Courts my grandparents encountered in the 1950s. It’s not the development my mother grew up in during the 1960s, and it’s not the development I remember from the 1970s.</p><p>What happened to LeClaire Courts is what happens to many communities that lack investment and opportunity. As the development’s buildings decayed, so did its connections to viable sources of education and employment. And the impact was dramatic. At age 35, the median earnings of Black children born to low-income parents in the census tract surrounding LeClaire Courts from 1978 to 1983 — just a decade or so after I was born — was just $19,740, according to data from <a class="Link" href="https://opportunityinsights.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Opportunity Insights</u></a>, a nonprofit think tank based at Harvard University.</p><p>This month, LeClaire Courts is being reborn as the CHA <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/09/04/construction-start-soon-long-vacant-leclaire-courts-cha-southwest-side" target="_blank" ><u>breaks ground on two residential buildings</u></a> on the former development’s site. Once the project is completed by 2028, there will be more than 180 units, <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2026/10/05/former-leclaire-courts-public-housing-redevelopment-to-break-ground-this-month/" target="_blank" ><u>with about half of them reserved for low-income renters</u></a>. In addition to the new construction, I hope there will be other forms of investment to help the next generation to grow up in LeClaire Courts find the economic stability that eluded the last generation to grow up there.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/author/alden-loury" target="_blank" ><i>Alden Loury</i></a><i> is data projects editor for WBEZ and writes a column for the Sun-Times.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a90000" name="module-a90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Welch's bluster on O’Hare project won't fly too far
entries.summary: <p>Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch raised some eyebrows after he attended a meeting in suburban River Forest to talk about the proposed O’Hare Flyer project, which would run express commuter trains back and forth from Downtown Chicago to O’Hare Airport.</p><p>Welch told attendees he could prevent two state agency budgets from moving forward if he didn’t get what he wanted out of the project for towns in and around his district.</p><p>Some residents of suburban towns along the route have expressed concern about the project, particularly about noise, and one person asked Welch at the meeting how opponents could stop the project or at least make it more difficult to complete.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ab0000" name="module-ab0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>“I can make it a little difficult,” Welch replied. According to the Oak Park Wednesday Journal, Welch pointed to the Illinois Department of Transportation and the Illinois Commerce Commission and said he could “let ‘em know that your budgets can be held up at budget time if you do things to negatively impact the communities that I represent.”</p><p>It seems kinda doubtful that the other Democratic leaders would agree to hold up IDOT’s huge budget over this, particularly since state money will play almost no role in building the project. The ICC’s main role in this project would be to approve railroad crossings. And railroads have an extraordinary amount of powers under federal law. If they want to build this with federal government help, it’s tough to stop them.</p><p>In other words, it was a lot like the playbook Welch used this year when he told the Chicago Teachers Union that he would take the lead on Chicago school funding during the veto session, and then later said he wanted a solution for all schools and then seemed to quietly drop the whole topic.</p><p>Welch signaled as much when he said, “I want to hear the good. I want to hear the bad,” according to the Oak Park paper. “I’m hearing from people in other communities that are in opposition. But I’m also hearing from people that are in support of this.”</p><p>So perhaps the usual political bluster. But publicly threatening to hold up entire agency budgets over nonbudget disagreements is not a common occurrence for a House speaker. That’s saying the quiet part out loud, and it rarely works well.</p><p>Since I mentioned the CTU earlier in this column, let’s get back to them.</p><p>As I’ve told you before, the CTU has been claiming that the state has more money for schools than it’s letting on. And as part of that argument, the union is demanding at least a billion dollars from the state during November’s veto session. That’s what Welch was responding to when he agreed to lead the charge for state funding next month.</p><p>And the CTU did so again after the release of a quarterly revenue report issued by the Commission on Government Forecasting and Accountability.</p><p>The commission reported robust quarterly growth in corporate income taxes and some other revenue sources totaling about $1 billion. But the commission’s report also warned: “While the first quarter produced strong revenue gains, several factors are expected to place downward pressure on revenues during the remainder of FY 2027 and could offset a significant portion of the gains realized thus far.”</p><p>For example, the Income Tax Refund Fund will be “$649 million lower” than last fiscal year, with the largest reductions coming in October and November. And another $349 million will be lost to the “annual reconciliation of business-related income tax receipt” which are known as “true-ups.” Another $265 million could be at least temporarily lost because of lawsuits filed against several new online-related taxes that were put into the budget.</p><p>The commission is also not convinced that the unexpected growth in corporate income taxes and sales taxes will continue, so “additional time and data are needed before the Commission updates its FY 2027 revenue outlook.”</p><p>The bottom line is that it could be quite dangerous to the budget to add a billion dollars in new spending before legislators even know how much money will actually flow into state coffers by late spring.</p><p>Welch’s upcoming reelection as House speaker is still in doubt, so numerous media outlets have claimed his nod to the CTU was an effort to bolster his position. But the O’Hare express train has support from several powerful statehouse groups, especially trade unions, which is a big reason it’s doubtful that those agency budgets will be stalled next spring.</p><p>So Welch’s bluster might help him a bit back in his district, but likely not under the dome when he fights to retain the speaker’s gavel in January.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-450000" name="module-450000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: DigitalMint's former employees ran $75 million cyber scam. Now, River North agency looks to have relaunched
entries.summary: <p>A River North cybersecurity firm seems to have started another business in the wake of a scandal involving two former employees and an associate who extorted tens of millions of dollars from customers.</p><p>The parent company of DigitalMint created a new website under Chaintrax Cyber, offering cybersecurity services to businesses, including negotiating ransomware cryptocurrency settlements, threat response and decryption.</p> <p>Documents filed Aug. 27 with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office show Chaintrax applied for a new trademark with the agency, paying application fees of $550, according to a filing made under parent company Red Leaf Chicago.</p><p>New York law firm Pryor Cashman and attorney Dyan Finguerra-DuCharme were listed as legal representatives. </p><p>The law firm declined to comment. Finguerra-DuCharme didn't respond to requests for comment.</p><p>The trademark application was filed less than two months after former DigitalMint employee Angelo Martino was sentenced to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/10/ex-chicago-ransomware-negotiator-gets-nearly-6-years-in-prison-for-aiding-hackers" >nearly six years in federal prison</a> for his role in extorting multiple victims in 2023. The 41-year-old Florida resident pled guilty in April to one count of conspiring to interfere with interstate commerce through extortion, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.</p><p>Martino conspired with former DigitalMint employee Kevin Tyler Martin and Ryan Clifford Goldberg, who worked for Israeli firm Sygnia Cybersecurity Services, according to prosecutors. </p><p>Martin, a 36-year-old Texas resident, and Goldberg, a 41-year-old Georgia resident, were sentenced in May to 48 months in prison.</p><p>Martino’s role in the scheme was to identify victims, extract data from their computers and lock their networks, while Goldberg identified computer weaknesses and gained access to victims’ networks. The trio would order companies to pay ransoms in exchange for a key to unlock encrypted data they hacked, promising not to publish the victims’ stolen data, prosecutors said.</p><p>The conspirators extorted more than $75 million from four companies and a nonprofit that Martino represented as a negotiator on behalf of DigitalMint, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/10/ex-chicago-ransomware-negotiator-gets-nearly-6-years-in-prison-for-aiding-hackers" >the Sun-Times previously reported</a>.</p><p>Martino and Martin were fired by DigitalMint. Goldberg no longer works for Sygnia.</p><p>A hearing to determine the amount of restitution Martino will be ordered to pay was rescheduled from Sept. 17 to Nov. 12, the Justice Department said.</p><p>It's unclear if DigitalMint has plans to rebrand as Chaintrax. The companies didn't respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Both firms are registered with the Illinois Secretary of State, have separate websites and contact information but offer similar services under the same executive team. </p><p>Marc Jason Grens serves as co-founder and president at both companies, while Jonathan Solomon is co-founder and CEO. Don Wyper is listed as chief operating officer. Chaintrax Technology Director Daniel Smith doesn't appear on DigitalMint's leadership team.</p><p>When there’s an incident within a company, leadership and culture take on added importance, according to Lynda Carlisle, partner at CS-Effect, a West Loop agency that handles crisis communications and related issues for businesses.</p><p>“If a brand’s reputation has been challenged, a discerning leader will look at the culture because the problems left could be carried over,” she said. “People are willing to try a new product or service. But if trust is broken, that sets off a different set of alarms that threatens client loyalty.”</p><p>Doyle Albee, who led communications for a Colorado technology company in the mid-1990s after its CEO went to prison for fraud, said reputational damage could last for years. In that scandal, whistleblowers tipped off local newspapers that the company inflated inventory sales by stuffing hard drives with bricks, recalling them for defects then reselling them to different customers.</p><p>“MiniScribe is still known here in Colorado as the company that shipped bricks,” said Albee, co-founder and managing director of public relations firm Prolexity in Colorado. “While the name change came from Maxtor's acquisition of MiniScribe rather than just a rebrand, the new name changed the sign on the building. It doesn't immediately change what shows up when people search, and it doesn't erase the mental association for customers who were burned.”</p><p>DigitalMint got its start in 2014 and became one of the largest bitcoin ATM operators in the country, with roughly 1,400 locations in dozens of states. But controversy quickly followed. </p><p>Bitcoin ATMs are often used by drug dealers and traffickers to launder money, as bitcoin can be hard to trace. And fraudsters often direct victims to send them crypto by using the ATMs to convert cash, officials say.</p><p>By 2016, Grens said the company found most of their customers making large crypto purchases were scam victims. </p><p>Grens, a Chicago native, ultimately shuttered the ATM business in 2024 — re-emerging DigitalMint as a cybersecurity consultancy and crypto payment service provider.</p><p>“I don’t want to build something dirty,” he told the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/01/17/cryptocurrency-crypto-fraud-scam-drug-dealing-trafficking-money-laundering-chicago-illinois" >Sun-Times in 2025</a> on why he left the ATM business.</p><p>Michael Shmarak, who teaches public relations at Northwestern University and is president of Northbrook PR firm Poetiq, said leadership should clearly differentiate the business entities.</p><p>“If DigitalMint is ceasing operations and sunsetting, then leadership needs to rip the Band-Aid off internally and externally to share why the company is changing trajectory,” he said. “Otherwise, customers and other stakeholders will be confused, leading to lost brand equity that competition will pounce upon.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/13/chicago-digitalmint-hack-ransomware-crime-angelo-martino-marc-grens" >Chicago cybersecurity firm employee brokered $75M in ransom after orchestrating hacks, feds say</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/01/17/cryptocurrency-crypto-fraud-scam-drug-dealing-trafficking-money-laundering-chicago-illinois" >Chicago’s crypto ATMs are magnets for drug-dealing and scams on older adults</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: After leveling playing field last season, Bears' Ben Johnson has chance to take control of Packers rivalry
entries.summary: <p>For decades, it was a bit of a stretch to call <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>-Packers a rivalry. It became such a one-sided domination that when former Green Bay quarterback Aaron Rodgers screamed, “I own you,” at Soldier Field in 2021 during yet another victory, the Bears didn’t have much to say back.</p><p>Even a diehard, lifelong Bears fan-turned-player had to concede.</p><p>“Well, I mean, let’s face it: He’s not totally wrong,” tight end Cole Kmet said a couple days later.</p><p>That's as bleak as it gets.</p><p>Rodgers used to chuckle about how each new Bears coach would talk about taking down the Packers, then sheepishly exit without having made a dent. Matt Eberflus went 0-5, Matt Nagy 1-7, John Fox 1-5 and the list goes on.</p><p>The last Bears coach to leave with a winning record against the Packers was Mike Ditka, who went 15-5 from 1982 through ’92. When the Bears visit Lambeau Field on Sunday, it’ll be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/09/1985-bears-championship-team-remembers-former-coach-mike-ditka-as-tip-of-the-spear" >their first game since Ditka died Friday at 86</a>.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson has been seeking to reestablish the tenacity the franchise played with under Ditka, and he got off to a good start in the rivalry by backing up the jab he made at his introductory news conference about beating Packers coach Matt LaFleur twice a season. The Bears lost their Week 14 game in Green Bay, then punched back two weeks later with a win at Soldier Field and another in the first round of the playoffs.</p><p>That could prove to be a pivotal point in the century-plus of this rivalry. The Bears have a lot left to prove, but they put themselves on even footing with the Packers last season. Johnson demolished the notion that the Bears were punching up when they faced that team, and they were done going into each season merely hoping to steal one.</p><p>Now they have an opportunity to fully turn the tables.</p><p>The Bears are riding high even with starting quarterback Caleb Williams sidelined by a hamstring injury, and the Packers look awfully vulnerable.</p><p>“We’re trying to turn this thing around, especially with the history of what it had been,” Bears running back D’Andre Swift said. “Any chance we get to go against them, it’s not something we take lightly. We know our fans don’t take it lightly.”</p><p>LaFleur is now feeling the heat after his team spiraled through a five-game losing streak, including both of those losses to the Bears, at the end of last season. Johnson has emerged as a legitimate villain in the saga, perhaps even a nemesis, with his, “[Expletive] the Packers” rant and icy post-game handshakes with LaFleur that are best measured in milliseconds.</p><p>LaFleur still has a 12-3 record against the Bears and the fourth-highest winning percentage among active head coaches, but Johnson has a chance to put him on his heels. Another win would make it four of the last five for the Bears and open the door to doubt in Green Bay leading up to the rematch at Soldier Field on Christmas.</p><p>The Bears haven’t won three consecutive games against the Packers since the 2005 and ’06 seasons under Lovie Smith.</p><p>The teams are headed in opposite directions at this juncture, though that could change quickly Sunday. As much as a win would fuel the Bears, a loss would deal a blow to their momentum and could shake the Packers out of their sluggishness.</p><p>But Johnson jolted the Bears last season with a complete reset of how they operated and led them to an 11-6 record and an NFC North title in his first season. They hadn’t finished above .500 since 2018.</p><p>LaFleur, meanwhile, couldn’t pull his team out of its nosedive at the end of last season and is off to a rough start in this one. His partner, quarterback Jordan Love, is struggling as well and currently sits at a 56.5 completion percentage and 86.5 passer rating.</p><p>The Packers are committed to those two after signing LaFleur to an unspecified contract extension. Love had already signed a $220 million deal through 2028.</p><p>They stumble into this game at 2-2, which has done nothing to soothe the fan base’s anxiety. The wins were narrow and ugly. The losses were absolute embarrassments.</p><p>The Packers opened the season by coughing up a lead in the fourth quarter — sound familiar? — against the Vikings on their way to a blowout loss. Two weeks later, they got destroyed at home by the Falcons, leading the Lambeau crowd to boo them throughout and leaving LaFleur to call it “a butt-whupping.”</p><p>In between, they squeaked by the Jets and Buccaneers — two of the worst teams in the NFL.</p><p>The Packers are near the bottom of the league in scoring and in the top 10 in most points allowed. They’re on pace for a historically bad rushing season. Love is meandering. LaFleur is short on answers.</p><p>That sounds a lot like some of the hapless Bears teams they used to beat up. And if the Bears are good enough to handle them again this season, the Packers will know exactly what that felt like.</p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: New Hyde Park painting honors late Chicago sculptor Richard Hunt
entries.summary: <p>A new three-story mural in Hyde Park honors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/12/16/24002254/richard-hunt-dead-chicago-artist-obituary" >the late sculptor Richard Hunt</a>, a lifelong Chicagoan and the first African American artist to receive a solo retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City.</p><p>The mural, created by Chicago artist Chris Devins, was installed early last week at 1515-19 E. 54th St., near several of Hunt’s sculptures and less than a mile from the Obama Presidential Center, where one of his final works, “Book Bird,” is installed.</p><p>Hunt was born on the South Side in 1935 and created more than 160 public works worldwide, including 35 outdoor sculptures in the Chicago area.<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/12/16/24002254/richard-hunt-dead-chicago-artist-obituary" target="_blank" > </a></p><p>Author and public historian Michelle Duster had been thinking about ways to honor Hunt for years. Duster, who is the great-granddaughter of Ida B. Wells, worked with Hunt for more than a decade as he created “The Light of Truth: Ida B. Wells National Monument” in Bronzeville. In 2021, she approached him about an honorary street name and a mural.</p><p>“I was like, ‘He needs to be honored,’” Duster said.</p><p>Hunt, who was receptive to the idea, died in December 2023, before the mural could be completed. Duster said she was crushed that he hadn’t lived to see it come to fruition, but his death only made her more determined to finish the mural.</p><p>“I made a promise to him that I was going to get this done,” she said.</p><p>The project took years of fundraising and searching for the right wall. Duster wanted a location connected to Hunt’s life and work and considered neighborhoods including Woodlawn, Englewood and Hyde Park. The 54th Street site ultimately was chosen because of Hunt’s ties to the area, including his affiliation with the University of Chicago and his work near the Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>Devins, who is known for his portraits of African American Chicagoans like Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Gwendolyn Brooks, met Hunt in 2023 after Duster connected the two. He spent several days photographing Hunt’s cavernous studio, filled with steel plates, hammers, anvils, car bumpers and a crane capable of moving pieces weighing thousands of pounds.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics/2019/8/2/20692194/chris-devins-murals-south-side-gwendolyn-brooks-jennifer-hudson-common-nat-king-cole-street-art" >South Sider creates ‘photo murals’ of artistic icons from Chicago’s black community</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“It really felt like walking into a Picasso studio or a French salon of some artists,” Devins said.</p><p>The photos Devins captured of Hunt in the studio became the basis for the mural.</p><p>Devins said the experience was particularly meaningful because his previous “Bronzeville Legends” project had featured people who had already died, meaning that he had relied on existing photographs of them.</p><p>“With him being still alive, I was able to catch him,” Devins said.</p><p>Duster described Hunt as soft-spoken, modest, warm and “the exact opposite of a diva,” despite his accomplished career. She recalled watching him interact with the audience at a 2023 screening of a documentary about his work, just months before his death, describing the exchange as one of “love and appreciation.” </p><p>“I felt like I was in the presence of somebody who was a giant when it came to what he contributed to the world, but his way of navigating the world was very understated,” Duster said. “I never met anybody like that before.”</p><p>For Devins, the mural is a way to ensure more people get to know the man behind the sculptures.</p><p>“Richard Hunt was a literal treasure to the city of Chicago,” Devins said. “We were lucky to have him.”</p>

entries.title: How we got this photo of the Northwestern Wildcats at the new Ryan Field
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist Manuel Martinez. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/nueli/" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>They say you only get one chance to make a first impression, so when Northwestern inaugurated its brand new Ryan Field, the challenge was to give the public a front row seat to this special day. It’s not often in sports that the game takes a backseat to the venue. On this day, the Wildcats defeated Penn State 34-13, but what most Chicagoans were most curious about was how $870 million dollars was spent on the new stadium. For this assignment, I was tasked with giving the public a behind-the-scenes look at the Wildcats' new home with images that not only captured the scenes of the day, but the excitement of fans and players. This image is the moment the Wildcat players ran through the tunnel and onto the field for the first time. What the image needed to convey was a sense of honor and pride for having been part of the inauguration of such a special new place — one that will carry the tradition of Northwestern football forward.</p><h3>How I got this photo:</h3><p>The most challenging part of creating this image is that while the tunnel run was a choreographed part of the game, no photographer had ever seen or done it on this field. Everything that day was happening as a first for both the players, fans and the journalists. Predictability is important photographers for successful images in a world that can be random. Everything was new — even simple things like moving from one side of the stadium to the other or remembering where the entrance to the field was. Moments before making this image, I photographed the upper bleachers of the stadium, capturing the flyover and a wide photo of fans and the stadium. I had to run from the 300-level seats all the way down to the field in 10 minutes. I positioned myself directly in front of the tunnel and photographed the players rushing out onto the field. The whole series of events took about one minute, but what this moment meant to the fans will last forever.</p><h3></h3><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul"
