entries.title: Chicago's older adults deserve answers, action about home repair funds
entries.summary: <p>A group of Chicago community organizations — <a class="Link" href="https://homeseniors.org/" target="_blank" >Housing Opportunities and Maintenance for the Elderly</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.accessliving.org/" target="_blank" >Access Living</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://northbranchworks.org/" target="_blank" >North Branch Works</a>, Mothers Opposed to Violence Everywhere, Illinois Anti-Foreclosure Coalition, <a class="Link" href="https://www.lightuplawndale.org/" target="_blank" >Light Up Lawndale</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.rebuildingtogether-chi.com/" target="_blank" >Rebuilding Together Metro Chicago</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.northsidecommunityresources.org/" target="_blank" >Northside Community Resources</a> — sent a letter to Mayor Brandon Johnson and city housing leaders over a month ago calling for an explanation for why $6.3 million allocated for the city’s Home Repair Program isn't being used for low-income seniors' critical home repairs and modifications. We are still waiting for answers.</p><p>In late 2024, the city closed the Small Accessible Repairs for Seniors program and folded its services into the Home Repair Program. The latter program provided safety and accessibility repairs to about 300 senior households every year.</p><p>Since then, seniors who were waiting for assistance through the Small Accessible Repairs for Seniors program have expressed that they are struggling to find help through the Home Repair Program.</p><p>Seniors are calling the city's 311 system and or their alderpersons for repairs that are urgent and dictate whether they can remain safely in their homes.</p><p>What is especially troubling is that some seniors are being directed back to community organizations that previously provided these services through the Small Accessible Repairs for Seniors program. These organizations had their funding eliminated when the program was closed.</p><p>If roughly $6.3 million in Home Repair Program funds remain available and they are being carried over into the next budget, seniors who need help now will suffer.</p><p>Illinois was designated an AARP age-friendly state last month. But we are not helping older adults if the city is leaving critical home repair resources unused. With the planning for the 2027 budget underway, the city needs to include funds to address the growing home repair need.</p><p>The city should provide a clear explanation of why these funds remain unspent, identify any restrictions on their use and determine whether eligible carryover funds can be directed toward residents facing urgent home repair needs.</p><p><i>Alizandra Medina, director of advocacy and neighborhood engagement, Housing Opportunities and Maintenance for the Elderly</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-430000" name="module-430000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Ishbia’s uninspiring Sox stadium plan</h3><p>Move over, Mighty Casey, because you’ve got company. Sox owner-in-waiting Justin Ishbia has struck out with his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/what-to-know-chicago-white-sox-stadium-proposal-justin-ishbia" >proposal</a> for a new stadium in the South Loop, failing to swing at the critical issues of location, design and tradition.</p><p>Stadium renderings shows exactly what Ishbia wants and where. If he has his way, Sox fans will either need to move within walking distance of his proposed park, or give up the generations-ingrained habit of driving to the games at 35th Street and Shields Avenue, as fans have been doing since, well, forever.</p><p>Aerial and street-level pictures of Comiskey Park for the first All-Star Game in 1933 show the ballpark surrounded by parking lots; the current stadium opened in 1991 with 70 acres of parking. If Ishbia did his due diligence, stadium renderings would have included surface parking lots to reassure fans. Instead, he may have to cobble together a route that includes Metra or the CTA. That, or fans will have to fork over a king’s ransom for Downtown parking.</p><p>Ishbia's design repeats the mistake of Rate Field's cantilevering multiple decks. That idea worked so poorly, the Sox were forced to remove eight rows of seating to create at least a faux sense of intimacy a la Comiskey.</p><p>Not only will Ishbia's stadium come with inadequate parking and nose-bleed seats, it likely will offer fewer seats altogether. Stadiums proposed or under construction for the Athletics, Tampa Bay Rays and Kansas City Royals have projected capacities of 31,000 to 34,000. Odds are likely Ishbia isn’t thinking of a venue seating 40,000-plus fans like Comiskey.</p><p>If only Ishbia were thinking of rebuilding Comiskey for the 21st century and beyond: Located in the neighborhood Sox fans know and love with updated engineering to reduce, if not eliminate, obstructed views while carrying upper decks down rather than away from the field — and with enough available land for mixed residential-commercial development and parking. That kind of plan would draw plenty of support.</p><p>The Railyards? Too bad this idea is way, way on the wrong side of the tracks.</p><p><i>Douglas Bukowski, Berwyn</i></p><h3>Hold federal immigration agents accountable </h3><p>Over a year ago, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/17/operation-midway-blitz-ice-arrests-little-village-fears-of-displacement-gentrification" >Operation Midway Blitz</a> launched in the Chicago area. Within a week, Silverio Villegas González was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/09/11/ice-shooting-silverio-villegas-gonzalez-chicago-franklin-park" >shot and killed</a> by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer during a traffic stop in Franklin Park. Weeks later, Marimar Martinez was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/10/05/marimar-martinez-lawsuit-trump-midway-blitz" >shot</a> five times by a Border Patrol agent in Brighton Park. In those two cases and in hundreds of other excessive force allegations, the federal government failed to investigate its agents' actions.</p><p>ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection are no less ruthless today, based on our findings at the Illinois Accountability Commission. The Department of Homeland Security has ramped up its quota-driven tactics across the country. ICE <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/ice-arrests-reached-record-highs-summer-enforcement-tactics-shifted-rcna596874" target="_blank" >arrested</a> 50,925 people in August alone — a monthly record. More than 300,000 people have been arrested by ICE this year. The detained population reached <a class="Link" href="https://tracreports.org/immigration/quickfacts/" target="_blank" >65,765</a> in July, and more than 70% percent of those individuals had no criminal conviction. DHS is now spending millions on <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/ice-electric-shock-gloves-85ff746d3e0ee5f39e7a9a3f1f576252" target="_blank" >electric shock gloves</a> so that agents can deliver more debilitating force with the swipe of a hand.</p><p>Last month, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/21/evanston-us-citizen-injured-federal-immigration-agents" >ICE agents in Evanston</a> wrongly detained a U.S. citizen and left him with injuries to his head, neck and teeth. In Alamo, Texas, agents <a class="Link" href="https://www.borderreport.com/border-report-tour/immigration/american-teen-who-posted-ice-raid-videos-sees-mother-deported/" target="_blank" >pepper-sprayed</a> a 17-year-old citizen and repeatedly struck another in the head for daring to film them. In Austin, Texas, an ICE officer shot an unarmed DoorDash delivery driver with a valid work permit in the back. To date, at least <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/08/us/immigration-agent-shootings-vehicles.html?eafs_enabled=false" target="_blank" >24 people</a> have been shot by federal immigration agents this year, including two fatalities in Houston and Biddeford, Maine, over the summer, and one in New York City last week. </p><p>When similar tragedies recur across the country, they require more than acknowledgment. The Illinois Accountability Commission spoke with witnesses and examined video, documents and official records and found patterns of indiscriminate enforcement unchecked by accountability. We transmitted our <a class="Link" href="https://secure-web.cisco.com/1WtWg5Dpfi91i5DttRXoP6CCW2u3dXdkkz90dnmfylyQEf0J3fkCbZHok4XNMCTl8ZeJLSac5dK-n2Mq6Fdp4E3Qo6SjgSmCaMT6mex4jKB4MRwkN-gcl7NoyPoXybWM78mPHbkjGYWcpas5sWyJ8Vb_M2LdwS4VZYkyE_TmNzxSzHe4aUD6hqm3mbrhisClJikBYMviP3ZM4fAl0ZcQbUAy48MTLN64IBiZHqzEzJXkUxuKvQ35LKe3W395bst64zGzRLHYrT0_Id33vuJpZJSnQrF54Sc9nzkY0udEjK_uNcTv5QGL274SIBe9ckn3O2Ee2qHN7Tb3jrcCHC05Q9Gr2_dm4Z83ASaQKX8A2Rr-cD_wrb-5s2JhbaqKZSwtLm58Z-v0-MJbbhUnVYq6xCniJeb42aYNEcpySe31K8eg/https%3A%2F%2Filac.illinois.gov%2F2026-04-iac-final-report.html" target="_blank" ><u>final report and referral letter</u></a> to state's attorneys and local law enforcement departments to support investigations and prosecutions of federal officers.</p><p>Communities are paying for the pattern. A recent University of Illinois Chicago study found that Cook County <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/09/08/uic-report-estimates-12b-retail-restaurant-activity-lost-during-heightened-immigration" target="_blank" >lost $1.26 billion</a> in retail and restaurant activity since immigration enforcement escalated. Trips to groceries, pharmacies and healthcare in affected neighborhoods fell nearly 8% with no signs of recovery, the study shows. People are delaying medical care. Parents are keeping children home.</p><p>The power to detain, arrest and use force carries the highest obligation of restraint. And when that fails to happen, as the Illinois Accountability Commission has well established, there must be accountability.</p><p><i>Rubén Castillo, chair; Hina Mahmood, executive director; and Ahmed Baset, lead counsel, Illinois Accountability Commission</i></p><h3>Solar power cuts Illinois energy costs</h3><p>Keeping the lights on is getting more expensive. One reason is something customers rarely see on their bills: the cost of ensuring enough power is available when needed most.</p><p>As Illinois' power grid operator, PJM Interconnection's responsibility is to make sure enough power is available across the region. Through its capacity market, power plants and other resources are paid to be available when needed. Utilities, like ComEd, are charged a share of those costs, which are then passed to customers.</p><p>With capacity prices reaching record highs, it’s worth asking what resources are already helping Illinois reduce its need for expensive power. One clear answer is distributed solar.</p><p>The amount ComEd customers pay toward PJM’s capacity market is determined by the five hours of the year with the highest electricity demand. During each of PJM’s five highest-demand hours last summer, solar projects built through the state incentive program Illinois Shines shaved about 900 megawatts off peak demand in ComEd territory. That is more than half the generating capacity of Illinois’ largest coal plant, Prairie State.</p><p>Illinois Shines has supported over 1,500 megawatts of solar across 69,000 systems in ComEd territory, including community solar projects, larger installations on businesses and industrial properties, and smaller systems on homes. Using weather and sunlight data to estimate system performance during peak hours, <a class="Link" href="https://votesolar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/DER-Performance.png" target="_blank" ><u>we found</u></a> an average output of about 913 megawatts, with estimated production ranging from 874 to 963 megawatts.</p><p>That matters because reducing peak demand can lower ComEd’s capacity costs, helping reduce costs passed on to customers. At the record $333.44 per megawatt-day capacity price for the 2027-2028 delivery year, reducing ComEd’s capacity obligation by roughly 900 megawatts could represent about $110 million in avoided costs annually.</p><p>The numbers point to a simple conclusion: Distributed solar was a major resource when electricity demand was highest.</p><p>And those benefits extend beyond households with solar panels. Renters, businesses and families who can't install their own systems can benefit when distributed solar reduces demand on the regional grid.</p><p>As Illinois faces growing electricity demand and record-breaking capacity prices, solar is reducing strain on the grid and helping lower energy costs for customers. It showed up when Illinois needed it, and its value will only grow as we commit to building more of it.</p><p><i>Kavi Chintam, Illinois campaign manager, and Will Kenworthy, Midwest regulatory director, </i><a class="Link" href="https://votesolar.org/usa/illinois/" target="_blank" ><i>Vote Solar</i></a></p><h3>AI’s uncertainty </h3><p>In 1942, the Manhattan Project sought to achieve a controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction, a crucial step toward building an atomic bomb. On Dec. 2, scientists succeeded in a squash court beneath the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. It was the first artificial, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.</p><p>Earlier theoretical discussions had raised concerns that the experiment might trigger an uncontrollable chain reaction or even a massive explosion. By then, however, most physicists considered those scenarios unlikely, though not impossible. The project nevertheless moved forward and ultimately produced the atomic bomb.</p><p>Long before COVID-19 pandemic, some scientists warned about the risks of certain kinds of viral research and laboratory safety. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.who.int/news/item/27-06-2025-who-scientific-advisory-group-issues-report-on-origins-of-covid-19" target="_blank" >unresolved origins</a> of the pandemic have only heightened those concerns.</p><p>Now we face another invisible frontier. Many scientists developing artificial intelligence warn that increasingly capable systems could outpace our ability to control them without adequate safeguards. Yet, as before, the momentum of discovery continues to drive us forward.</p><p>It sounds like science fiction to imagine machines deciding they no longer need us and disabling their creators in the name of efficiency or survival. Still, humanity seems to have a habit of spinning the cylinder in a technological game of Russian roulette, hoping it lands on an empty chamber.</p><p><i>Scott T. Thompson, Bloomington, Indiana</i></p><h3>JB isn’t my jam </h3><p>So, former Illinois House Republican Leader Jim Durkin wants us to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/05/ex-illinois-house-gop-leader-jim-durkin-endorsement-gov-jb-pritzker-over-darren-bailey" >vote for JB Pritzker</a> because he’s a “good person, and he has delivered on matters important to me and the state.” What matters are those? From my point of view, JB has only raised my taxes (gas, groceries, tolls), done nothing to lower property taxes (Illinois' are among the highest in the nation), and the only businesses I see coming to the state are gambling and marijuana establishments. Those are the "matters" important to me, and I’m sure they are for many others. It's reason enough to say "enough" and vote against Pritzker.</p><p><i>Barbara Piltaver, Schiller Park</i> </p><h3>Fact dodger </h3><p>In the movie “A Few Good Men," Lt. Daniel A. Kaffee, played by Tom Cruise, is interrogating Jack Nicholson's Col. Nathan R. Jessep, regarding an illegal hazing punishment that led to a private's death. The line, “You can’t handle the truth” reminds me of the reason President Donald Trump is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/09/24/trump-media-ban-republicans-cnn-ap-ms-now-politico-cupp" >restricting</a> CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from White House access. The president, in his bubble, only accepts information that is not critical of his words and deeds. He can't handle the truth.</p><p><i>Samuel Solomon, Deerfield</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Widower considers chances with kissing cousin
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a man in his 60s who lost his wife two years ago to a heart attack. I have fallen in love with my cousin, who is also in her 60s, divorced and a lawyer. Is it reasonable for me to ask her to go with me on dates? Can a man marry his first cousin? — <i>CONFUSED IN NEW JERSEY</i></p><p><b>DEAR CONFUSED:</b> According to the free legal reference website Justia (law.justia.com), first cousins are not listed among the types of forbidden marriages or civil unions in the state of New Jersey. In other words, yes, it seems to be legal where you live.</p><p>Even so, you will want to tread very carefully here. You say you've fallen in love with her, but are you sure she has romantic feelings for you? If not, you risk alienating a family member you deeply respect and admire.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have two brothers, "Derek" and "Paul," who have not spoken to each other in more than six years. There was no falling-out; they're simply bad at communicating (even with other siblings). Last year, Derek wanted to get together with all the siblings, but Paul wouldn't come (no reason given).</p><p>I just found out that Derek has terminal cancer. He doesn't want Paul to know. I assume it has to do with Paul not wanting to get together, which hurt Derek's feelings. I believe Paul should be told about Derek's condition. What is the best way to get Derek to reconsider informing Paul of his diagnosis? — <i>IN THE MIDDLE</i></p><p><b>DEAR IN THE MIDDLE:</b> You and your family have my sympathy for Derek's condition. It's not wise to assume anything in a situation like this. If you want to know why Derek is keeping his cancer a secret from Paul, ask him. Tell him you're there for him and will help him break the news if he would like.</p><p>Meanwhile, approach Paul to plan a sibling get-together that would fit his schedule. If he still refuses, it's likely these two have problems you're unaware of that go beyond poor communication skills.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I recently took a friend on a day trip. While I was driving, she took out her clippers and trimmed her fingernails in my car. Later, when she changed into her walking shoes, she put the soles of these shoes on the dash of my car to tie them. Thank goodness there wasn't a pebble stuck in the bottom, or my dashboard would have been scratched in addition to the dirt. I was dumbstruck that someone would do this in someone else's nice car. What is a good way to ask that these things stop? I was unprepared and without words. — <i>BOTHERED IN THE WEST</i></p><p><b>DEAR BOTHERED:</b> The most effective way to have delivered the message to your disrespectful friend would have been to say, clearly and firmly, "Excuse me! I don't want footprints on my dashboard or nail clippings in my car." Follow it up by asking her to clean up both messes.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</p>

entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Mary Ellen Guest made sure the mission of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobungalow.org/" target="_blank" >Chicago Bungalow Association</a>, as much as it was about the brick-and-mortar gems central to the city's DNA, was really about the people who lived in them.</p><p>Before she was hired as executive director in 2008, the non-profit centered on celebrating and preserving the unique architectural style of Chicago bungalows, which account for a third of the city's single family housing stock.</p><p>"Mary Ellen transformed our The architectural style accounts for a third of the city’s single family housing stock.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tom Cruze/Sun-Times file </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“She took the white gloves of preservation off. She made preservation practical and accessible, helping homeowners get what they needed to stay in their homes and make them safer, more comfortable, and affordable to live in,” Wineman said.</p><p>Ms. Guest died Sept. 20 from health complications following a fall. She was 71.</p><p>The association, which receives part of its funding from the city, was created by Mayor Richard M. Daley (who grew up in a bungalow) in 2000 to help preserve and maintain the city's iconic homes. It has more than 68,000 members. </p><p>"She really had the ability to connect on an individual level with members and understand their true needs, and she always stayed true to her "meet you where you are" approach," said Wineman, who is serving as interim executive director.</p><p>Membership, which is free, nearly quadrupled under Ms. Guest's watch.</p><p>Ms. Guest was especially proud of focusing membership growth in underserved communities on the South and West Sides. </p><p>She attended up to 80 events a year in spaces ranging from church basements to community centers to spread the word about the many ways the non-profit could help with things like connecting homeowners to energy efficiency programs, trusted contractors and funding sources.</p><p>She also expanded the scope of the association's mission to include older homes that were not bungalows.</p><p>"Everybody she worked with loved her, and she was tireless, she'd work all day at their office in the Monadnock Building and then be beating the drum out in the community," said Tom Murphy, a founding board member of the association.</p><p>"For better or worse home ownership is the path to wealth building in this country and has been for a long time and Mary Ellen took pride in helping steer resources to working-class neighborhoods to preserve housing stock," said Chris Meister, a longtime friend who serves as auditor general of the state of Illinois.</p><p>Ms. Guest also oversaw a "Stop the Pop" campaign that began in 2016 against "pop top" expansions of bungalows — so named because they "pop" off the lower roof of a bungalow and replace it with a much larger, usually squared-off, second floor.</p><p>The group believes the approach sacrifices the quintessential look of a bungalow for the sake of space.</p><p>To change minds, they offered two preferred alternatives to second floor additions that emphasize thoughtful design but cost about the same, if not less, than a full "pop."</p><p>The campaign marked just how far appreciation for the bungalow had come. When the association was founded, bungalows were unfashionable and "thought of as your grandma's house," Guest <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/7/8/18417467/group-offers-renovation-options-to-preserve-look-of-historic-chicago-bungalows" target="_blank" >told the Sun-Times in 2018</a>.</p><p>When she took the helm, the group's title was the "Historic Chicago Bungalow Association." Ms. Guest lopped off the word "Historic" to emphasize its active and forward-thinking mission.</p><p>But she made sure paying homage to the history of the bungalow remained key, overseeing an expansion of <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobungalow.org/historic-districts" target="_blank" >National Register Bungalow Historic Districts</a> in the city.</p><p>Ms. Guest was born Aug 3, 1955, to Ronald and Helen Guest. He was a dispatcher for a trucking company. She worked as a medical librarian for a hospital.</p><p>Ms. Guest grew up on the Southwest Side and attended the now-closed Queen of Peace High School and earned an education degree from Chicago State University.</p><p>In 1982 she got into political campaign work, starting as a volunteer and working her way up to head the campaign office for Adlai Stevenson III's unsuccessful 1982 gubernatorial campaign.</p><p>She worked on a number of other campaigns, including Richard M. Daley's unsuccessful mayoral run in 1983 and his first two successful mayoral campaigns in 1989 and 1991, for which she became known as the "Queen of the Phone Banks" by recruiting and organizing hundreds of volunteers to work the phones.</p><p>She later served as executive director of Working in the Schools, a Chicago non-profit that promotes literacy, and A+ Illinois, a coalition that advocated for equitable school funding reform.</p><p>"She was such a positive and wonderfully warmhearted person who served as a mentor to lots of people and really was like the glue who got people to stick together and work together on things," said friend and political strategist Pete Giangreco, who worked in the campaign trenches with Ms. Guest.</p><p>"And she was a force," he said. "You didn't want to be on the other side of a righteously indignant Mary Ellen."</p><p>Ms. Guest loved baking, her Irish heritage, attending the South Side Irish parade and her two sons whom she raised as a single mother in the Beverly area.</p><p>"The throughline for her was just a deep, deep care and love for other people and dedicating herself to doing things for others," said her son James Schulte. "Her grandparents came here from Ireland and she carried the immigrant's perspective of self sacrifice to advance the next generation."</p><p>In addition to her son James, Ms. Guest is survived by her son John Schulte, as well as two grandchildren.</p><p>Services have been held.</p>

entries.title: Rising fuel prices another blow to Chicago restaurants
entries.summary: <p>Chicago restaurants are being squeezed from all sides as surging fuel prices drive up the cost of food and supplies, while higher household costs are prompting consumers to eat out less.</p><p>Several food suppliers have significantly raised their fuel surcharges, an added fee for clients to help cover fuel costs, as diesel prices climb amid the war in Iran. The average price of diesel in Chicago was $6.86<b> </b>per gallon on Friday, up more than 68% from a year earlier, according to AAA. Diesel prices in the city reached its highest average price of $7.02 on Sept. 26.</p><p>“Everything we do comes in on trucks, right? All our supplies come in on trucks,” said Kevin Vaughan, owner of Vaughan Hospitality Group, which owns six bars and restaurants across Chicago, including Chicago Brewhouse and Corcoran’s Grill & Pub. “For example, food — beef, produce, etc. — there's a huge impact on those industries because diesel is up so high and transport is up so high. So we're starting to see that accelerate.”</p><p>Vaughan's suppliers have said their freight charges are going up dramatically and will continue to be passed onto restaurants. One of his suppliers charges a $9 fuel surcharge when diesel costs $5 to $5.49 per gallon. Every time diesel increases by 50 cents, the supplier increases the surcharge by $1. </p><p>Vaughan also believes consumer demand is falling as higher gas prices squeeze household budgets.</p><p>“This is anecdotal, but I feel as if people are not necessarily going out as often … and [it's] all driven by fuel and other things like interest rates, the cost to rent, etc.,” Vaughan said. “The consumer is feeling big pressure on managing their budgets.”</p><p>A KPMG survey from April found 67% of consumers are eating at home more often than dining out, with the majority citing budget concerns as the primary reason. When consumers do dine out, 25% said they're frequenting quick-service or fast-food restaurants, shifting away from casual and fine dining options.</p><p>Mario Ponce, restaurant consultant with Chicago-based Partners in Hospitality, said he's seeing a similar shift among his clients, with consumers trading casual sit-down restaurants for cheaper options such as fast-food, pizza and sandwich shops.</p><p>Ron Cain, owner of Kuma’s Corner, said sales at the burger restaurant are down 15% and 11% in the past four months, compared to the year before, for his Avondale and Schaumburg locations, respectively.</p><p>“Our Schaumburg location has been consistent since we opened in 2015, and this is the first year we're really feeling an impact on the traffic,” Cain said.</p><p>Although sales are down, Kuma’s Corner is absorbing their cost increases, rather than passing them down to customers. These include rising beef prices due to the national cattle herd shortage, as well as suppliers’ fuel surcharges, Cain said.</p><p>But the trade-off is tricky. He said customer traffic is low, so raising prices might help, but it could reduce traffic further.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-030000" name="image-030000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/99b7dc8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F28%2F56%2Fd02ec21a4c438c37037e14fddd58%2Fkumascorner-260430-04.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f83dd6b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F28%2F56%2Fd02ec21a4c438c37037e14fddd58%2Fkumascorner-260430-04.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/daac115/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F28%2F56%2Fd02ec21a4c438c37037e14fddd58%2Fkumascorner-260430-04.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Kuma’s Corner at 2900 W. Belmont Ave.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“You can only charge so much for a burger,” Cain said. “So we have not passed down the cost of our margins.”</p><p>Instead, the restaurant is focusing on appealing to customers by offering temporary special deals and discounts that encourage them to dine out.</p><p>Some new offers include half-sized lunch burgers, mac and cheese and a beer for $12 on Mondays and a chicken sandwich with fries and a beer for $15 on Tuesdays. Kuma’s also launched a chicken caesar wrap on Sept. 1, which received 340 orders on DoorDash in the first month. Cain said they plan to sell the wrap with fries and a beer for $14.</p><p>“We're doing that on a limited time basis, hoping that the economy's going to turn around at some point, you know, hoping this war is going to end and the fuel prices are going to come down,” Cain said.</p><p>At Vaughan’s establishments, prices for beef menu items have increased while other costs are being absorbed by the company. Beef prices have squeezed his business the hardest, Vaughan said.</p><p>Fuel is also impacting the cost of plastic products, such as cups, since those are petroleum-based products, Vaughan said, adding another strain to his restaurants’ costs.</p><p>Sam Toia, president of the Illinois Restaurant Association, said small, independent and family-owned restaurants are particularly vulnerable because they have less buying power than larger restaurant chains and are seeing larger increases in fuel surcharges.</p><p>“If they were open six days a week, maybe they're open five days a week,” Toia said. “If they're open lunch and dinner, maybe they're just open dinner … because the only two things you can control in the restaurant business is labor costs and food costs.”</p><p>Despite such measures, Toia feels restaurant closures will be inevitable if fuel prices remain high and economic pressures persist. </p><p>Cain is also worried.</p><p>“I mean, that's my main concern — surviving all this nonsense,” Cain said.</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Tyson Bagent has chance to write his name in rivalry lore
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Tyson Bagent walked off the field Sunday with a familiar song blaring from the Soldier Field speakers.</p><p><i>Country roads, take me home/To the place I belong</i></p><p><i>West Virginia, mountain mama/Take me home, country roads</i></p><p>The Martinsburg, W.Va., native almost cried.</p><p>“It's extremely humbling,” he said.</p><p>The win against the Jets was emotional for the Bears quarterback, who was making his first start in three years, and for his family in the stands.<br>Sunday’s game against the Packers on Sunday will be emotional for the entire fan base, though. Like Walter Payton 27 years earlier, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/10/09/mike-ditka-dead-bears-coach" target="_blank" >Mike Ditka</a> — the Pro Football Hall of Fame tight end and legendary coach — died during Packers week. The Bears’ best tribute to Ditka would be with by beating the rival he — and everyone still inside Halas Hall — hate so much.</p><p>In 1999, six days after Payton’s death, the Bears saluted Payton at Lambeau Field when Bryan Robinson blocked Ryan Longwell’s 28-yard field goal as time expired. That win improved the Bears to 4-5 and snapped a 10-game losing streak against the Packers.</p><p>“I think Walter Payton picked me up,” Robinson said then, “because I can’t jump that high.”</p><p>A win Sunday would improve the Bears to 4-1 and wrest control of the rivalry into coach Ben Johnson’s arms, perhaps for years to come. Even against a struggling Packers team, the Bears will need Bagent to play better than he did last week to walk out of Lambeau Field with a rare victory.</p><p>"Every game ever given to me, nothing changes on my end,” Bagent said. “It is very cool to be able to play in the greatest rivalry in sports.”</p><p>Bagent went 25-for-34 for 268 yards and an interception in the 23-12 win against the Jets, but had three more interceptions come back because of penalties. He leaned on the NFL’s best rushing attack — one that will look different Sunday. With running back Kyle Monangai out with an injured toe, the Bears will lean on D’Andre Swift, who was benched against the Jets after fumbling for the second time in three games.</p><p>A team that struggled in short yardage and in the red zone last week could also turn to Roschon Johnson, a power runner who will take Monangai’s place. More than anything, though, they’ll need Bagent to be accurate and on time when it matters most.</p><p>That’s a lot of pressure for Bagent, the son of an arm wrestler and the team’s second-string quarterback since they made him an undrafted free agent out of Div. II Shepherd University. It might be his last chance to start for a while, too — Caleb Williams, who has spent three weeks rehabbing his injured hamstring, returned to practice Friday for the first time.</p><p>Bagent proved last week — and third-stringer Case Keenum the week before — that the star of the Bears’ offense might just be the offense itself.</p><p>“It's great to see their opportunity come and those guys just execute what you thought they would be able to do,” offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. “It's a great way to send the message across the team. ‘This is what it looks like, this is the expectation.’ Because there was never a doubt in anybody's mind that whoever played in whatever week was ready to go. </p><p>"To see that come to light has been pretty cool.”</p>

entries.title: Man found fatally shot in Garfield Park home
entries.summary: <p>A man was found shot to death in the hallway of a Garfield Park home early Saturday. </p><p>The man, 26, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in the 3600 block of West 5th Avenue around 1:35 a.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said. His name hasn't been released. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p>

entries.title: 2 teen boys shot in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>Two teenage boys were shot while sitting in a car late Friday in Englewood on the South Side. </p><p>The boys, 16, were inside the parked car in the 6500 block of South Laflin Street when a motorcycle drove by and the driver opened fire around 11:20 p.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>One boy was struck in the buttocks and was taken to Comer Children's Hospital in good condition, police said. The other boy was struck in the foot and was taken to Little Company of Mary Hospital. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p>

entries.title: Trump's Medicaid cuts strip refugees and other legal immigrants of their health coverage
entries.summary: <p>New restrictions have stripped Medicaid coverage from certain legal immigrants, including refugees and victims of human trafficking, as part of <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/1e2b12a91a3d12ceb0420ce7053de58e" target="_blank" >broader federal changes</a> to the health insurance program that are expected to force millions off their coverage.</p><p>The change effective Oct. 1 cut from Medicaid what is estimated to be hundreds of thousands of people who legally immigrated to the United States, many of whom work and pay taxes, in the latest <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/2d631ee59e141da4cf471817ef414829" target="_blank" >Trump administration policy</a> to target foreigners.</p><p>The move is part of sweeping changes to Medicaid under President Donald Trump’s 2025 <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/125ad670515460108ded062029abd8c8" target="_blank" >tax cut and policy law</a>, with many set to take effect early next year. The Medicaid changes are projected to result in 7.5 million fewer people with health insurance, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s 2025 estimate.</p><p>Advocates say that without Medicaid, people will not be able to afford private insurance and will either delay care or end up in emergency rooms, adding pressure to strained health system. For immigrants, the cuts could be felt more acutely, compounding the effects of other administration efforts to restrict their access to public assistance as part of a <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/immigration" target="_blank" >broader immigration crackdown</a>.</p><p>“This is about telling every immigrant in the United States that they are not welcome here and that they should leave,” said Ben D’Avanzo, a senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, which has pursued litigation against the Republican administration over its immigration agenda.</p><p>Refugees, asylum seekers, victims of human trafficking and domestic violence are among those who have lost coverage. Green-card holders were not impacted.</p><p>Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that “immigrants must be able to support themselves without taking from overburdened benefits programs paid for by hard-working American taxpayers.”</p><p>D’Avanzo said many people who have lost coverage will likely only realize when they need medical care. But for some, the change has been felt immediately.</p><h3>Dwindling supplies of lifesaving medication</h3><p>In Tucson, Arizona, María Chacon has been caring for her son Jesus for almost five years since a car accident at 17 left him unable to breathe on his own. He requires a ventilator, a feeding tube and daily medication, and must be turned once every two hours to stop sores from forming. Chacon said he sometimes opens his eyes.</p><p>The family is originally from Mexico and entered the U.S. on a T visa, offered to victims of human trafficking, in 2018.</p><p>Chacon said Medicaid has helped cover almost $25,000 per month of care for her son, which includes a small stipend for her and her husband as compensation for being long-term caregivers. She said doctors have explained that even if they both worked 24 hours a day, they would not be able to cover the cost of his care.</p><p>“Since that day I haven’t been able to sleep. We haven’t been able to eat or anything. We're wondering what we’re going to do?” Chacon said.</p><p>Jesus takes medication that Chacon estimates costs $7,000 a month. The supply runs out in mid-October. Without coverage, she does not know how her son is going to survive.</p><p>Chacon found out just days before the cuts that she was losing care. She called the state's Medicaid offices to appeal. Although she is in the process of obtaining a green card, Medicaid coverage would only kick in five years after she is approved.</p><p>Steven Camarota, research director for the Center for Immigration Studies, a right-leaning think tank that seeks less immigration, said the administration “is trying to nibble around the edges” with the Oct. 1 cuts, finding piecemeal ways to curb immigration into the U.S.</p><p>Camarota believes the government should screen legal immigrants for income potential and education, reducing the number who might rely on public benefits once they cross the border.</p><p>“You need immigrants who are unlikely to need welfare,” he said, or those with high educational attainment.</p><p>The administration recently revived a federal rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits that could include food stamps, Medicaid, housing vouchers and others.</p><p>Chacon believes the cuts to Medicaid coverage are part of the administration’s clampdown on immigrants. She said her son is in no condition to travel.</p><p>“I know that’s what he’s doing, but, as my son is, I couldn’t go to Mexico,” Chacon said.</p><h3>Millions more will be dropped from Medicaid</h3><p>Medicaid, jointly funded by states and the federal government, has become a political focal point during Trump’s second term. The president has pushed to root out what he describes as fraud in the program. In July, the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/medicaid-fraud-minnesota-california-oz-rfk-trump-24033ef9807b46f8b6fd6614ef5b1169" target="_blank" >administration deferred</a> over $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, claiming there was suspected fraud; critics argued the move targeted Democratic-led states.</p><p>As more people are cut from Medicaid, the federal government is predicted to reduce program spending by $911 billion, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.</p><p>In Arizona, officials said 29,000 legal immigrants were cut from Medicaid rolls on Oct. 1. In Florida, estimates are closer to 177,000. Overall, more than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are estimated to lose Medicaid coverage, according to KFF.</p><p>As more states implement various restrictions to coverage, 7.5 million people are expected to lose coverage by 2034, according to analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.</p><p>Without coverage, people will turn to emergency rooms for care. When people delay seeing a doctor, conditions can worsen and become even more expensive to treat.</p><p>“At the end of the day, it does raise the cost for the states because once you get these people in for something that could have been prevented, they could not go to the doctor because they were uninsured; they most likely will end up at a hospital in an emergency room,” said Carmen Feliciano, the vice president of policy and advocacy at UnidosUS, a Latino civil rights organization.</p><p>UnidosUS partners with community organizations to help provide medical care, but Feliciano said they already are overwhelmed and would not be able to support the number of people who are going to lose medical coverage in the coming months.</p><p>“We are not going to have the capacity to serve all the people who need it,” Feliciano said.</p>
